The right for personal autonomy is, roughly speaking, freedom of the person to chose to not participate in someone else's rituals or any activities.

Imagine you live in a great community. One day the members come to your home and say that they are going to dance under the moon to summon the rain. You don't want to go and say that you're busy. One possible scenario is they say ok, fine, it is up to you, although, you know, you're going to benefit from that rain too, but anyways, you don't have to go if you don't want to. This would mean you have personal autonomy. But if they say that you have to participate because everybody has to participate, and everybody has to participate because 2/3 voted that everybody has to participate, or 2/3 of those who voted voted that everybody has to participate, or a single representative elected once in a year by 2/3 of those who voted...

This doesn't mean that a murderer or a thief is able to tell community to fuck off, because they already violated someone's right and thus waived their own rights.

"But everybody agreed on these rules", "Democracy is shit but it is the best what we have".

Most probably the core of human rights should be enforced. But the core is small. It can be written in several pages, call it a bill of rights, a constitution, commandments, whatever. It is a short list of simple rules that can be generalized as 'do not be a jerk' or 'do not exploit others' or 'do not spend someone's energy'.

What is outside of the core doesn't have to be enforced. A person should be able to say no to any so-called legislation/regulation that he did not vote for, to taxes, to conscription, to public schools, to vaccination, to insurance, etc.
